items.q: Amortized complexity of appending to a Python list, and why isn't it O(n)?
items.a_short: O(1) amortized. The list over-allocates, so most appends are free and the occasional O(n) resize is spread across them.
items.a_full: Growth is geometric (roughly 1.125x for large lists in CPython). Over n appends the total copy work is O(n), so the average per append is O(1). Any single append can still be O(n).

items.q: When do you reach for two pointers?
items.a_short: Sorted array (or one you can sort) where you need a pair/triplet meeting a condition, or in-place partitioning.
items.a_full: Signals: 'sorted array', 'pair that sums to', 'remove duplicates in place', 'container with most water'. It turns an O(n²) nested loop into O(n) by exploiting the ordering — move the pointer that can improve the result.

items.q: What signals a sliding-window problem?
items.a_short: 'Contiguous subarray/substring' plus a constraint — longest, shortest, or a fixed size k.
items.a_full: Fixed window: slide and update in O(1). Variable window: expand right until the constraint breaks, then shrink from the left. Each element enters and leaves once, so it's O(n) even though there are two loops.

items.q: Two Sum in one pass — what's the key idea and complexity?
items.a_short: Store each value's index in a hashmap as you go and look up the complement `target - x`. O(n) time, O(n) space.
items.a_full: The general pattern: trade space for time by remembering what you've already seen, so each element only needs an O(1) lookup instead of a scan.

options: Sort then binary search, O(n log n)

items.q: What is 'binary search on the answer'?
items.a_short: When the answer space is monotonic — a candidate either works or doesn't, and feasibility only flips once — binary search over candidate answers rather than array indices.
items.a_full: Signals: 'minimum capacity to ship in D days', 'smallest divisor', 'minimize the maximum'. Write a `feasible(x)` predicate that's monotone, then binary search x. Complexity is O(n log(range)).

options: Binary searching over candidate answers using a monotone feasibility test

items.q: What problems does a monotonic stack solve?
items.a_short: 'Next greater/smaller element' style questions — largest rectangle in histogram, daily temperatures, trapping rain water.
items.a_full: Keep the stack increasing or decreasing; when the incoming element breaks the order, pop and resolve those elements — the incoming one is their answer. Each element is pushed and popped once, so it's O(n).

items.q: Top-k largest from n elements — which approach and why?
items.a_short: A min-heap of size k: O(n log k) time, O(k) space. Beats sorting (O(n log n)) when k << n.
items.a_full: Push each element, pop the smallest whenever the heap exceeds k. Quickselect gives O(n) average but O(n²) worst case and needs the whole array in memory — the heap works on a stream.

options: Min-heap of size k, O(n log k)

items.q: BFS vs DFS — when does the choice actually matter?
items.a_short: BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs and explores level by level; DFS is for connectivity, cycles, topological order and backtracking.
items.a_full: BFS uses a queue and O(width) memory; DFS uses a stack (or recursion) and O(depth) memory. On a wide shallow graph DFS is cheaper; on a deep narrow one BFS is. If the question says 'shortest' and edges are unweighted, it's BFS.

options: BFS for shortest path in unweighted graphs; DFS for connectivity/cycles/backtracking

items.q: What is a topological sort and when is it impossible?
items.a_short: A linear ordering of a DAG where every edge u→v puts u before v. Impossible if the graph has a cycle.
items.a_full: Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take nodes with in-degree 0. If you process fewer than n nodes, a cycle exists — this doubles as cycle detection. Classic uses: course scheduling, build dependency order, layer ordering in a compute graph.

options: Impossible when the graph has a cycle

items.q: What is Union-Find good for, and what's its complexity?
items.a_short: Dynamic connectivity — grouping elements and asking 'same set?'. Near O(1) amortized with path compression plus union by rank.
items.a_full: Formally O(α(n)), the inverse Ackermann function, which is under 5 for any practical n. Uses: Kruskal's MST, counting connected components, detecting cycles in an undirected graph, 'number of islands' variants with incremental updates.

items.q: Memoization vs tabulation.
items.a_short: Memoization is top-down recursion plus a cache; tabulation is bottom-up iteration filling a table.
items.a_full: Memoization only computes states you actually reach and is easier to write from the recurrence. Tabulation has no recursion limit, better constants, and allows space optimization — keeping only the last row or two instead of the full table.

options: Memoization is top-down with a cache; tabulation is bottom-up

items.q: 0/1 knapsack: recurrence, complexity, and the space trick.
items.a_short: `dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w-wt[i]] + val[i])`. O(nW) time and space, reducible to O(W) by iterating weights downward in a 1-D array.
items.a_full: Iterate w from high to low so each item is used at most once. Iterating low to high instead gives the unbounded knapsack, where items can repeat. Note O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial — it's exponential in the number of bits of W.

options: O(nW) time, reducible to O(W) space

items.q: Longest Increasing Subsequence — the O(n log n) method.
items.a_short: Maintain `tails[i]` = smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length i+1; binary search each element's insert position.
items.a_full: The `tails` array is always sorted, so `bisect_left` finds where the element goes. Its final length is the LIS length — but the array itself is not a valid LIS, so reconstructing the actual subsequence needs parent pointers.

options: Sort and compare, O(n log n)
Patience/tails array with binary search, O(n log n)

items.q: What's the general backtracking template?
items.a_short: Choose → explore → un-choose, with a base case that records a complete solution.
items.a_full: Forgetting `path[:]` is the single most common bug — you append a reference to a list that keeps mutating. Pruning with `valid()` is what turns brute force into something that finishes.

items.q: How does Floyd's cycle detection work, and how do you find the cycle's start?
items.a_short: Slow moves 1, fast moves 2. If they meet there's a cycle. Then reset one pointer to head and move both one step at a time — they meet at the cycle entry.
items.a_full: The second phase works because the distance from head to the cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point to the cycle start, modulo the loop length. O(n) time, O(1) space — the whole reason to use it over a hash set.

options: Slow/fast pointers, then reset one to head

items.q: Merge overlapping intervals — approach and complexity?
items.a_short: Sort by start, then sweep: if the current start <= last end, extend the last end; otherwise push a new interval. O(n log n).
items.a_full: `max(out[-1][1], e)` matters — a fully-contained interval would otherwise shrink the merged range. Almost every interval problem starts with sorting by start or end.

options: Sort by start then sweep, O(n log n)

items.q: What does a prefix-sum array buy you?
items.a_short: O(1) range sums after O(n) preprocessing: `sum(i..j) = pre[j+1] - pre[i]`.
items.a_full: Combined with a hashmap it solves 'subarray sums to k' in O(n): store counts of each prefix sum seen, and for each new prefix look up `prefix - k`. The 2-D version is the integral image used in classic computer vision.

options: O(1) range sums after O(n) preprocessing

items.q: When is a trie the right structure?
items.a_short: Prefix queries over a set of strings — autocomplete, 'does any word start with', word search on a board.
items.a_full: Lookup is O(L) in the key length, independent of how many words are stored, which beats a hashmap when you need prefixes rather than exact matches. Cost is memory: a node per character, though it shares common prefixes.

options: Prefix queries over a string set

items.q: What does Quickselect do and what's its complexity?
items.a_short: Finds the k-th smallest element in O(n) average by partitioning and recursing into only one side. O(n²) worst case.
items.a_full: Same partition step as quicksort, but you discard the half that can't contain k, so the work is n + n/2 + n/4 ... = O(n). Random pivot selection makes the worst case vanishingly unlikely; median-of-medians guarantees O(n) but with bad constants.

items.q: When does Dijkstra fail, and what do you use instead?
items.a_short: It fails with negative edge weights. Use Bellman-Ford, which also detects negative cycles.
items.a_full: Dijkstra's correctness rests on the assumption that once a node is finalized no shorter path exists — a negative edge can break that later. Complexity with a binary heap is O((V+E) log V); Bellman-Ford is O(VE).

options: Fails with negative edge weights; use Bellman-Ford

items.q: In-order, pre-order, post-order — which is which, and what's each for?
items.a_short: In-order L→Root→R (sorted output for a BST), pre-order Root→L→R (serialize/copy a tree), post-order L→R→Root (delete, or compute from children up).
items.a_full: Post-order is the one to reach for when a node's result depends on its children — height, diameter, subtree sums. Level-order (BFS) is a fourth option, used when you need to work by depth.

options: In-order gives sorted output for a BST
Pre-order gives sorted output for a BST
All three give the same order

items.q: Why is this BST validation wrong?
items.a_short: It only checks parent-child pairs, not the full subtree range. A node deep in the left subtree can exceed the root and still pass.
items.a_full: Tree [5, 1, 6, null, null, 4, 7] passes this check but isn't a BST — 4 sits in the right subtree of 5. The fix is to pass down a (low, high) bound and narrow it at each step.

options: It only checks immediate children, not subtree bounds

items.q: How do you get O(1) get and put in an LRU cache?
items.a_short: Hashmap from key to node, plus a doubly linked list for recency. The map gives O(1) lookup, the list gives O(1) move-to-front and evict-from-tail.
items.a_full: A singly linked list won't do — you need the previous pointer to unlink in O(1). In Python, `collections.OrderedDict` with `move_to_end` gives you both for free, and `functools.lru_cache` is the ready-made decorator.

items.q: Two strings are anagrams — fastest check?
items.a_short: Compare character counts: O(n) with a 26-length array or a `Counter`. Sorting is O(n log n).
items.a_full: For a fixed small alphabet the count array is O(1) space. For grouping anagrams, the sorted string or the count tuple becomes the dictionary key.

items.q: What do `x & (x-1)` and `x & -x` give you?
items.a_short: `x & (x-1)` clears the lowest set bit; `x & -x` isolates it.
items.a_full: Counting set bits by repeatedly doing `x &= x-1` runs in O(number of set bits) rather than O(bit width). `x & -x` is the core of a Fenwick tree. Also: `x ^ x == 0` powers the 'single number among pairs' trick, and `x & (x-1) == 0` tests for a power of two.

options: Both isolate the lowest set bit
x&(x-1) clears the lowest set bit; x&-x isolates it

items.q: Merge sort vs quicksort vs heapsort — the trade-off table.
items.a_short: Merge: O(n log n) guaranteed, stable, O(n) extra space. Quick: O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst, in-place, unstable, best cache behaviour. Heap: O(n log n) guaranteed, in-place, unstable, poor locality.
items.a_full: Real libraries blend them: introsort is quicksort that switches to heapsort on deep recursion; Timsort is merge sort exploiting existing runs. Quicksort usually wins in practice on arrays because of cache locality, despite the worse bound.

options: Quicksort is O(n log n) worst case
Merge is stable with O(n) space; quick is in-place but O(n²) worst case

items.q: Reverse a singly linked list iteratively.
items.a_short: Walk the list keeping `prev`, `curr`, `next`; point each node backwards. O(n) time, O(1) space.
items.a_code:
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    while head:
        nxt = head.next
        head.next = prev
        prev = head
        head = nxt
    return prev
items.a_full: Save `next` before you overwrite `head.next` — losing it is the classic bug. The recursive version is elegant but O(n) stack, which matters for long lists.

items.q: Why does deep recursion fail in Python, and what do you do about it?
items.a_short: Default recursion limit is 1000 frames and CPython has no tail-call optimization. Convert to an explicit stack, or raise the limit carefully.
items.a_full: `sys.setrecursionlimit` raises the Python-level cap but not the C stack, so too high a value segfaults. For tree/graph work on large inputs, rewrite DFS with an explicit stack — it also makes the state easier to inspect.

options: No TCO and a ~1000 frame limit; use an explicit stack
The limit is unlimited by default

items.q: How do you cut a 2-D DP table to O(n) space?
items.a_short: If `dp[i]` only depends on `dp[i-1]`, keep two rows (or one, iterating in the right direction).
items.a_full: Direction matters: for 0/1 knapsack you iterate weights downward so each item is counted once; for unbounded knapsack you go upward. Space optimization usually destroys your ability to reconstruct the solution path — keep the full table if the question asks for the actual subsequence.

options: Keep only the rows the recurrence depends on

items.q: Common patterns for 2-D grid problems?
items.a_short: BFS/DFS flood fill for regions, a direction array for neighbours, in-place marking to avoid a visited set, and layer-by-layer walking for spiral/rotate.
items.a_full: `DIRS = [(0,1),(1,0),(0,-1),(-1,0)]` keeps neighbour code clean. Mutating the grid (e.g. setting visited cells to '0') saves O(mn) space but destroys the input — ask whether that's allowed.

options: Flood fill with a direction array; mark in place to save space

items.q: What's the complexity of building a heap from n elements — and why isn't it O(n log n)?
items.a_short: O(n). Sift-down from the middle up: most nodes are near the leaves and sift down only a level or two.
items.a_full: The sum Σ(n/2^h)·h over heights converges to 2n. Inserting one at a time really is O(n log n) — `heapq.heapify` uses the linear method, so prefer it over a loop of `heappush`.

items.q: You're stuck on a coding question in an interview. What's the recovery sequence?
items.a_short: State the brute force out loud with its complexity, solve a tiny concrete example by hand, then name what's wasteful about brute force — that's where the optimization lives.
items.a_full: Brute force on the whiteboard is worth far more than silence: it shows you understand the problem and gives the interviewer something to hint against. Most optimizations come from one of three moves — sort to expose structure, hash to remember what you've seen, or two pointers/window to avoid rescanning.

options: Stay silent until you see the optimal solution
State the brute force and its complexity, then identify the waste
